form: Abstract: The article covers the specific features of Salish toponyms, namely the main toponymic groups of oronymes, hydronymes and oikonymes represented in the dictionaries of Salish languages. A typological feature of the Salish language toponymic system is the presence of microtoponyms, that is, individual names of small objects. The author distinguishes a distinct type of mythologized toponyms, the majority of which are mythologized oronyms - specific mountain peaks, localities, individual rocks, and hills associated with Salish geomyths. The specificity of the Salish toponymic system is represented in context of the theory nominative types of the Russian linguist E. Berezovich. Unlike the oronyms and oikonyms of the Salish languages, which demonstrate predominantly ancient models of nomination of situational and combinatorial nominative types, the semantic system of hydronyms is mostly taxonomic and gradational.

form: It should be noted that A. Matveyev, the prominent Russian linguist who studied toponyms, considered oronyms to be the most archaic in the linguistic picture of the world; they routed the map - that is, the objects of places that were important to ancient people, and, thus, performed an aesthetic, mythological-religious function, they were kind of a memorization technique, helped with orientation, served as the most important sources of information: “The man is characterized by anthropocentrism, therefore, for him, the point of reference is the man himself, at the heart of everything is a comparison with the man. If a complex of objects was immediately in the field of view, as, for example, usually happens in the mountains, the comparison was made with an entire group of people, which could also include animals (or vice versa). Consequently, orography is most favorable for the implementation of the name-creation; on the contrary, it is usually not possible to keep a complex of hydro objects in the field of view” (Matveev 1987).

form: Berezovich E.L., the prominent Russian linguist who has been studying the toponymic systems, following Matveyev A.K., notes that the distribution of situational names in the toponymy of various peoples, such as Finno-Ugric, Caucasian, Turkic, is natural. Such names are associated to a greater extent with nomadic life than with agricultural life: “these names are much more widely represented in those toponymic systems for which verb (participial) constructions are characteristic” (Berezovich 1998). And further Matveyev indicates that there is reason to believe that the first toponyms arose from descriptive constructions such as ‘The mountain on which there are bears’ (= ‘Bear Mountain’). The Salish languages of nomadic North American hunter-fishermen represent such a diachronic stage since such structures were likely primary in the language's diachrony. Hence it can be assumed that the type of the Salish situational toponyms is the most ancient.
